adolescents who engage more frequently in online risky behaviors are more likely to be cyberbullying victimized, while those who engage more frequently online risky behaviors are at greater risk of being cyberbullying victimised compared to traditional bullying.

cyberbullying victimizations were more likely to occur in adolescents who engaged more frequently in online risky behaviors, such as online risky leisure activities, risky online lifestyle activities, online risky social networking, and online risky gaming, than in those who engaged less often in these behaviors.

adolescents' engagement in online risky leisure activities, online risky social networking, and online lifestyle activities were associated with cyberbullying victimizations, and adolescents who engaged in online risky social networking and online lifestyle activities had a higher likelihood of cyberbullying victimizing than traditional bullying victimization.

adolescents who engage in risky online leisure and online lifestyle activities and who do not practice cybersecurity management are more likely to be cyberbullied than those who engage less frequently in the same behaviors.
adolescents who engaged more frequently in online risky behaviors and less frequently in cybersecurity management were more vulnerable to cyberbullying victimizations.

adolescents who engage in risky online leisure and online risky social activities are at a greater risk of cyberbullying than traditional bullying, and that adolescents who engage more frequently in online lifestyle activities are at a higher risk of cyberbully victimization than traditional bullying victimization.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cyberbullying is not a separate form of bullying, but is rather an extension of traditional bullying.
cyberbullying victimizations can be predicted by adolescents' online risky behaviors and online cybersecurity management.
adolescents who engage in online risky behaviors and who do not have a good cybersecurity management plan were at higher risk for being victimized by both cyberbullying and bullying.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cyber routine activities theory can be applied to cyberbullying research and that online risky behaviors can be used to identify cyberbullying subgroups.
adolescents who engage in risky online leisure and risky social networking activities may be more vulnerable to cyberbullying victimizations than traditional bullying victimizations.
cyberbullying and bullying victimization should be considered separately because the two types of victimization are associated with different risk factors.
